# Gravel Bike

## Overview

The gravel bike is the one I ride most, because it copes with the towpath behind the house and the broken lane that leads to the next village without complaining. It is an aluminium frame weighing 10.4 kg with the pedals on, which is not light, but it is tough and the weight has never been the thing that slowed me down. The geometry is relaxed enough for a long day and sharp enough to be fun on the rough stuff. I built it up from a frameset over a winter, so I chose every part, and I have only changed a couple of things since. Everything on it is a compromise between speed on tarmac and grip on loose stone, and those compromises suit the riding I actually do. That is the whole point of the bike. It is not the fastest thing I own and it is not the lightest, but it is the one that means I never have to decide what kind of ride I am going on before I leave the house. I can take the towpath to the next town, join the road for the last few miles, and come home on the broken lane, all on the same bike and the same set of tyres.

## Setup

The tyres are the heart of the setup. I run 38 mm tubeless tyres, which is the width that lets me drop the pressure without pinching and still roll well on tarmac. Front sits at 32 psi and rear at 35 psi, which is a few pounds more at the back to carry my weight and the load. Going tubeless means the sealant handles the small punctures that used to mean a tube change at the roadside. I set the pressures with a proper gauge rather than by feel, because a rear tyre a few pounds soft is the difference between a quick ride and a sluggish one.

The drivetrain is 1x11, with a 42 tooth chainring at the front and an 11-42 cassette at the back. One chainring means one shifter and no front derailleur, which is one less thing to adjust and one less thing to drop a chain on rough ground. The range is enough for the hills around here, though I do spin out on the steepest descents. The drop bars have a 20 degree flare, so the hoods stay narrow for the road and the drops are wide enough to steer with confidence when the surface turns loose. The brakes are hydraulic discs, which I would not trade for anything on the wet lanes. I keep a small pump on the frame, because tubeless tyres still lose pressure over a week and checking before a ride is easier than discovering a soft tyre at the gate.

## Maintenance

Every three months I top up the sealant in both tyres, because it dries out with time and a tyre without sealant is just a tubeless tyre waiting to puncture. I check the rotors for wear and give the pads a look while the wheels are off, and I check the wheels for loose spokes at the same time. The cables get a pull at the barrel adjusters when the shifting starts to feel slack, and I replace the inner cables once a year whether they need it or not. The bearings get a check at the same service, bottom bracket and headset and hubs, since a rough bearing caught early is a cheap fix and a seized one is not. I clean the drivetrain with a brush and re-lube the chain after wet rides, which is most of them in winter. I keep a written card in the shed with the sealant date and the last time each wheel was off, because nothing on a bike wears out so quietly as a tyre that has been losing sealant without anyone noticing. The drivetrain gets a full clean once a month in the wet season, and I replace the chain when a check on the wear tool says it is due, since a worn chain wears the cassette and the chainring with it. The frame gets a wash whenever the mud dries on it, mostly so I can see the paint underneath and spot a crack early. The wheel bearings and the headset get a hand-feel check at each service, and I re-grease the hub bearings once a year.

## Troubleshooting

A tyre that burps air usually means the pressure was too low for the load, or the bead was not seated properly when it was fitted. I reinflate to a higher pressure and reseat the bead, then let it back down. Rear shifting that goes wrong under load is almost always cable tension, so I adjust the barrel adjuster half a turn and re-test. If it is still slow on the upshift I check the derailleur hanger, because a bent hanger is the common cause and it is easy to knock on a rough descent. A creak from the seatpost is the one that fools people, since it sounds like it comes from the bottom bracket. I clean the post and the seat tube, apply a little carbon paste if it is a carbon post, and re-torque the clamp, and that normally settles it. A tyre that will not hold pressure at all is usually a bead that never seated rather than a puncture, so I reinflate hard once to seat it and listen for the pop before I go looking for a hole. If the brakes start to feel spongy, the fluid has taken on water and wants bleeding, which is a twenty-minute job I do rather than live with.

## Notes

The bike is deliberately unfashionable. Aluminium, mechanical gears, nothing electronic, and no part I cannot replace at home. The 38 mm tyres do most of the work of smoothing the ride, which means the frame does not have to be clever. If I built it again I would keep everything the same except the bars, where I might go a shade wider. The one thing I would warn anyone about is the pressures. Copying someone else's numbers is a mistake, because they depend on your weight and your load, and the right figure is the one that stops the tyre squirming without feeling wooden. I would also tell anyone buying their first gravel bike to spend the money on the tyres and the wheels before the frame, because those two things change how the bike feels far more than the tube set does. The bike has done two winters now and the only parts I have replaced are the chain, the brake pads, and one set of tyres, which is a cheaper record than I expected when I built it. If I ever sold everything else in the shed, this is the bike I would keep, because it is the one that gets used when I am not sure what the day holds.
